page: Amazon Web Services g4dn.metal is a bare-metal accelerated computing instance built for graphics-intensive and machine learning workloads. It features two Intel Xeon 8259CL processors delivering 48 physical cores and 96 vCPUs running at 2.5 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. Memory capacity stands at 384 GB of DDR4 RAM clocked at 3 GHz, maintaining a balanced 4 GB per virtual core. Hardware acceleration is provided by eight NVIDIA Turing T4 GPUs providing a cumulative 128 GB of GDDR6 VRAM. Local storage consists of an integrated 1800 GB NVMe SSD, complemented by a 100 Gbps baseline network interface.

Benchmark results demonstrate exceptional multi-core and memory throughput. Multi-core performance metrics in stress-ng and PassMark place in the upper quartile, paired with uncached memory read bandwidth exceeding 219 GB/sec and cached bandwidth reaching 4548 GB/sec. Synthetic data operations show strong throughput, with Redis SET operations recording over 77 million operations per second and high static web serving capabilities. However, single-core metrics across Geekbench and stress-ng fall into the middle percentile due to the conservative 2.5 GHz base clock, reflecting an architecture focused on parallel throughput rather than raw single-thread speed.

From an infrastructure efficiency standpoint, the bare-metal architecture removes hypervisor overhead, providing direct access to the underlying hardware and maximum GPU utilization. The integration of eight discrete accelerators alongside high-speed local NVMe storage and 100 Gbps networking provides high resource density on a single physical host, minimizing multi-node networking complexity for mid-scale distributed jobs.

This server is primarily suited for batched machine learning inference, distributed video transcoding, cloud graphics rendering, and concurrent database workloads that benefit from dedicated host resources and localized GPU acceleration.

Without virtualization overhead, the server delivers high resource density for multi-GPU pipelines, rendering clusters, and large-scale parallel processing.
